Faire face au racisme pour la première f: Facing Racism for the First Time
“Tu sais d’où tu viens, tu sais qui tu e: “You know where you come from, you know who you are, you know your dad is a Québécois, you know your mom is Congolese, you know you’re mixed.”
Pour les personnes racisées, se retrouve: For racialized people, finding yourself the victim of discrimination is rarely an isolated incident. The people we spoke with, who touched on issues ranging from microaggressions to hateful remarks, illustrated with their stories those first childhood confrontations with racism.
Schaël Marcéus, un jeune homme de 26 ans: Schaël Marcéus, a 26-year-old man of Haitian origin, remembers in detail an incident he experienced when he was 8. “The Winnie the Pooh movie had just come out, and I had a Tigger figurine. I brought it to daycare,” he says. “I was with an educator and I said to her: ‘Look, Hélène, it’s you.’ And I did a pirouette, figurine in hand,” he recalls. Schaël remembers that the day went by completely normally. “When my parents came to pick me up, the educator asked to speak with them in her office. She asked them about what I watched on TV, asked whether they kept an eye on me and whether I watched shows that weren’t appropriate for my age.” A popular show at the time had triggered this worry. “The week before, there had been a character in an episode who was a voodoo master,” Schaël explains. “The educator thought I was practising voodoo. I still remember the fear in her eyes.”
Elvira Kamara, une Afropolite ivoirienne: Elvira Kamara, a 35-year-old Ivorian Afropolitan, went through something similar, having become the target of her teacher at age 11. “I had just arrived in France and I was the only Black person in my class,” she says. “The homeroom teacher, a nun, made me introduce myself in front of the whole class because, according to her, I came from Africa. She was shocked by the quality of my French,” she recalls. Elvira was the only student who had to introduce herself to all her classmates this way.
Pour Elizabeth Tran, une native de Montr: For Elizabeth Tran, a 32-year-old Montréal native, the first experience of racism goes back to elementary school. She was seven. “I had brought a Vietnamese dish for lunch. A kid asked me what it was called. I didn’t know the translation of the dish’s name. They laughed at me, saying I didn’t know what I was eating.”
Yara El-Soueidi, une Libano-Québécoise d: Yara El-Soueidi, a 29-year-old Lebanese Quebecer, was confronted with another student’s racism in Secondary 4, at a private school in Montréal. “This was during the reasonable accommodation crisis,” she says. “I was putting my things away, and someone threw something at me.” The attacker was a boy in her class. “It was a fairly heavy metal object. It could have hurt me,” she explains. “I turned around and asked him why he did that. He told me that because of ‘people like me,’ people couldn’t do what they used to do anymore, and that they were being forced to be like us.” The young Yara didn’t quite grasp what her classmate was saying, or what she said to him. “He answered that I wasn’t Québécoise, that I was just a ‘dirty Arab.’”
Pour Zaynab, qui a 27 ans, plusieurs inc: For Zaynab, who is 27, several incidents also occurred in elementary school. “Kids once told me my skin was black because my mother pooped on me when she gave birth to me,” she reports. On two occasions, students’ discriminatory behaviour was not sanctioned by school staff. “A boy called me a dirty n**** on the school bus.
I saw red. I jumped on him. Obviously, I’m the one who got in trouble, even though that boy was older and bigger than me, and I couldn’t have hurt him.”
Le scénario se répète au secondaire. « O: The scenario repeated itself in high school. “We were supposed to go outside and I told the boy in front of me to follow the instructions and get in line.” For all answer, Zaynab received a violent punch to the face. “Guess who got in trouble,” she concludes.
Sephora, une femme noire non-binaire âgé: Sephora, a 35-year-old Black non-binary woman, lived through a traumatic experience on the way home from school when she was 9. At the time of the assault, she was on the bus with her father. “I had my backpack, I was wearing my school uniform,” she remembers. “A seat opened up next to a woman on the bus. I came over to sit down and she put her hand against my chest to stop me. She pushed me to the side to move me away, saying: ‘No, not you.’ Then she motioned to a stranger, a white woman farther back, to come and sit down.” Sephora’s father reacted immediately.
« J’ai regardé mon père, qui s’est mis à: “I looked at my father, who started yelling: ‘I saw what you did, ma’am! You’re racist, that’s not okay, you don’t do that to a child.’” Nobody intervened. When they reached their stop, Sephora and her father got off the bus. “Nobody explained to me what had just happened, that the incident I had just been through was racist and that I hadn’t done anything wrong,” she laments. “I never forgot it.”
Naadei Lyonnais, qui est Noire, a grandi: Naadei Lyonnais, who is Black, grew up in Rouyn-Noranda. She remembers an incident that happened a week after she arrived in the city. She was six at the time. “I was walking with my mother and a car stopped in the middle of the street,” she says. “The passengers were staring at us and pointing; their eyes were wide with surprise. They surely didn’t mean us any harm.
C’était probablement la première fois qu: It was probably the first time they had seen a Black person, but at six years old, it left a huge mark on me.”
Très jeune, Naadei a développé un mécani: At a very young age, Naadei developed a defence mechanism against the discrimination directed at her. “At six, after several incidents, I decided I simply wouldn’t see racism, that I wouldn’t think about it, that I wouldn’t assume it existed, that I wouldn’t talk to my parents about it,” she says. “I would simply erase that idea from my mind, reject the concept. That’s why, when I experienced discrimination, I chose to think that people just didn’t like me personally, for no particular reason,” she explains. She says she made that choice after realizing very early on that racism was everywhere, even among people she loves, including her friends and family. “I understood right away that if I paid attention to it, I would feel sadness, frustration or, worse, hatred. So, to protect myself and be happy, I decided to block all of it out.”
Maricar-Kristine Montes, une jeune femme: Maricar-Kristine Montes, a 27-year-old woman of Filipino origin born in Quebec, also recalls events that marked her daily life as a child. She remembers witnessing the discrimination her parents faced, including the way they were sometimes treated in stores. “I was very young, but it was plainly visible,” she says. “Since we weren’t from here, I internalized the idea that these were things I should expect. We always kept our heads down, or we acted like nothing had happened.” When her family settled in a Montréal suburb, Maricar was six. She quickly became the target of her classmates’ disparaging remarks, which hadn’t been the case when she went to school in Côte-des-Neiges.
« Les élèves faisaient constamment des b: “The students constantly made jokes about Black people, Asians, Latinos and Muslims. Anything that was different from them, it was okay to make fun of it.” In high school, she spoke out angrily for the first time against a particularly disgusting comment. “A student told me I didn’t need to sign up for CEGEP, because I was going to end up working at Thaï Express.” Instead of condemning such behaviour, she was told: “That’s not what he meant,” “You’re too sensitive” and “Come on, it was funny!” “Nobody tried to reassure me. They just defended him,” she regrets.
Lorsqu’on constate les difficultés que p: When you see the difficulties racialized children can go through, you understand the urgency of acting. The artist Joyce N’sana knows something about this. A musician and mother of two children aged seven and eight, she is a member of <l1>Biblio Afro Jeunesse</l1>, a collective that promotes children’s books with racialized characters and anti-racist books for kids. “People started following the page because it features books written by racialized authors. But we don’t want it to be only racialized parents or parents from diverse backgrounds who sign on; this initiative is also meant for other parents. Everyone has to feel concerned by the problem in order to raise children who are anti-racist,” she says. One of the page’s contributors is, in fact, a white Quebecer man. “That matters enormously too, so that parents realize it’s not only a page for racialized people. It’s for everyone, because fighting racism doesn’t happen through just one community, it happens through all communities.”
D’après Mme N’sana, les écoles manquent: According to Ms. N’sana, schools lack structure when it comes to anti-racism. “They just tell themselves that kids tease each other, and it’ll pass. When kids live it every day and there’s no structure, or parents who are aware enough of the issue to educate their children, it doesn’t pass,” she believes. The artist, who is also a childhood educator, began tackling the subject with children very early on. “People aren’t born racist, they become racist. It’s about behaviours and intolerances that get reproduced because they were observed somewhere. Children just repeat what they see, which is why it’s important to start educating children about these topics very young,” she elaborates. And when it comes to children, it’s often simpler than we think. “People wonder how they’re going to do it, because these are complex subjects. But if you explain them to little ones, if you correct them, it’s enough for them to understand.”
Il faut commencer par des choses très si: You have to start with very simple things and speak their language. “My kids and I have had our share of incidents,” she confides. “My son came home from school one day saying: ‘I want you to cut my hair.’” Inspired by his mother, he wore locs at the time. “But when he got to school, his friends told him they weren’t nice, that they were poo. ‘I want to cut them,’ he kept saying.” Joyce and her son talked it over, and he calmed down. Unfortunately, a few days later, the remarks started up again, worse than before, and the boy went and got the scissors himself to cut his hair. His brother also had to deal with difficult situations at school. “My eldest got called ‘Chinese,’” she says. “I told him: ‘You know where you come from, you know who you are, you know your dad is a Québécois, you know your mom is Congolese, you know you’re mixed.’ When he came to me crying with this story, I said to him: ‘Do you remember what we talked about? At school, there are only two of you, you and your brother, with a different skin colour. The others may have never seen that before. Maybe all your friends at school know about ‘diversity’ is Chinese people. But you have a mouth, you’re able to explain it to them. Is your skin the same colour as someone from China? So explain it to your friend,’” she recounts.
Son garçon a suivi les conseils de sa mè: Her son followed his mother’s advice in his own way, though not before she had explained to him that Chinese people are to be treated with respect, like everyone else, and that he shouldn’t hurt another friend. Ms. N’sana also believes that reading can greatly help children understand the society they live in. “In a book, you can convey a lot of things,” she sums up. Given current events, a selection of anti-racist books for children has also come out. To finish, she reminds us of something of great importance. “We target children, but first and foremost, we have to address parents, because they’re the ones who can educate children. If parents aren’t educated, they can’t talk to their children about this issue. Structures like schools, libraries, daycares and CPEs should be able to put in place programs and initiatives to raise awareness among parents and children about racism and diversity.”
Et vous, quelle a été votre première exp: And you, what was your first personal experience with racism? What do you do to fight it?
